question: Under what condition may cylinders of compressed gas be loaded in a horizontal (lying down) position?
choice_a: Never; cylinders must always be loaded upright
choice_b: Only if the cylinder is designed so the relief valve is in the vapor space
choice_c: Only if the cylinders are less than half full
choice_d: Only during cold weather transport
explanation: The manual states cylinders may be loaded in a horizontal position if it is designed so the relief valve is in the vapor space.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-11

question: Where must a driver never load a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD?
choice_a: In a separate sealed compartment away from the cab
choice_b: In the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption
choice_c: Anywhere in the trailer regardless of other cargo
choice_d: Only on cargo tanks over 1,000 gallons
explanation: The manual prohibits loading a package labeled POISON or POISON INHALATION HAZARD in the driver's cab or sleeper, or with food material for human or animal consumption.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: What is the maximum total transport index allowed for all Class 7 (Radioactive) packages loaded together in a single vehicle?
explanation: The manual states the total transport index of all packages in a single vehicle must not exceed 50.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

topic: Do Not Load Table - Poisons and Food
question: According to the Do Not Load table, when can a Division 6.1 or 2.3 poison-labeled package be loaded in the same vehicle as animal or human food?
choice_a: Never, under any circumstances
choice_b: Only if the poison package is over-packed in an approved way
choice_c: Only if the food is in sealed cans
choice_d: Only if the food is for animal consumption, not human
explanation: The Do Not Load table permits loading a Division 6.1 or 2.3 poison-labeled package with animal or human food only if the poison package is over-packed in an approved way.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

topic: Do Not Load Table - Cyanides and Acids
question: Why must Division 6.1 cyanides or cyanide mixtures (such as Silver Cyanide or Sodium Cyanide) never be loaded with acids or other acidic materials?
choice_a: The acid could corrode the cyanide packaging
choice_b: The combination could release hydrocyanic acid
choice_c: It voids the shipper's certification
choice_d: Federal law bans mixing any two Division 6.1 materials
explanation: The Do Not Load table prohibits loading cyanides or cyanide mixtures with acids, corrosive materials, or other acidic materials which could release hydrocyanic acid.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: What is the key difference between a cargo tank and a portable tank as bulk packaging?
choice_a: Cargo tanks are permanently attached to the vehicle and remain on it when loaded/unloaded, while portable tanks are loaded and unloaded off the vehicle
choice_b: Portable tanks can only carry gases; cargo tanks can only carry liquids
choice_c: Cargo tanks require an EPA permit; portable tanks do not
choice_d: There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable
explanation: Cargo tanks are bulk packaging permanently attached to a vehicle and remain on it when loaded and unloaded, while portable tanks are loaded or unloaded off the vehicle and then put on a vehicle for transportation.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: What are the two most common types of cargo tanks described in the manual?
choice_a: DOT-406 and DOT-407
choice_b: MC306 for liquids and MC331 for gases
choice_c: Type A and Type B portable tanks
choice_d: IM-101 and IM-102
explanation: The manual states the most common cargo tanks are MC306 for liquids and MC331 for gases.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: How must identification numbers be displayed on bulk packaging such as cargo tanks and dump trucks?
choice_a: Black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white diamond-shaped background if no placards are required
choice_b: Red numbers stenciled directly on the tank shell
choice_c: Any color numbers at least 1 inch tall
choice_d: Numbers are only required on the rear of the vehicle
explanation: The rules require black 100 mm (3.9 inch) numbers on orange panels, placards, or a white, diamond-shaped background if no placards are required.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-12

question: On a portable tank with a capacity of more than 1,000 gallons, how tall must the letters of the shipping name be?
choice_a: At least one inch tall
choice_b: At least two inches tall
choice_c: At least four inches tall
choice_d: No minimum height is specified
explanation: The letters of the shipping name must be at least two inches tall on portable tanks with capacities of more than 1,000 gallons, and one-inch tall on portable tanks with capacities of less than 1,000 gallons.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-13

question: While a cargo tank of hazardous material is being loaded or unloaded, how close must the qualified person watching it remain?
choice_a: Within 10 feet
choice_b: Within 25 feet
choice_c: Within 50 feet
choice_d: Within 100 feet
explanation: The person watching the loading or unloading must be within 25 feet of the tank, alert, have a clear view of it, and know the hazards and emergency procedures.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-13

question: Before moving a cargo tank of hazardous materials, what must be done regardless of how small the amount or how short the distance?
choice_a: All manholes and valves must be closed
choice_b: The tank must be completely emptied
choice_c: The placards must be removed
choice_d: The tank must be refilled with nitrogen
explanation: Manholes and valves must be closed before moving a tank of hazardous materials to prevent leaks; it is illegal to move a cargo tank with open valves or covers unless it is empty according to 49 CFR 173.29.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-13

question: Before filling a cargo tank with flammable liquid through an open filling hole, what must the driver do?
choice_a: Turn on the engine to power the pump at full speed
choice_b: Ground the tank correctly and maintain the ground until after closing the filling hole
choice_c: Remove all placards from the vehicle
choice_d: Disconnect the tank from the trailer frame
explanation: The driver must ground a cargo tank correctly before filling it through an open filling hole, and maintain the ground until after closing the filling hole; the engine must also be turned off before loading or unloading unless needed to operate a pump.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-13

question: After a cargo tank of compressed gas has been uncoupled from the power unit, what must the driver do to prevent motion?
choice_a: Leave the parking brake off so it can be moved quickly
choice_b: Chock the trailer or semi-trailer
choice_c: Leave the liquid discharge valve open
choice_d: Disconnect the placards
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to always chock trailers and semi-trailers to prevent motion when uncoupled from the power unit, and to keep liquid discharge valves closed except when loading and unloading.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-13

question: How close to the traveled part of the road may a vehicle carrying Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives ever park?
choice_a: It may never park within five feet of the traveled part of the road
choice_b: It may park as close as two feet if hazard lights are on
choice_c: There is no minimum distance requirement
choice_d: It may park directly on the shoulder at any time
explanation: The manual states you must never park with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives within five feet of the traveled part of the road, and except for brief operational necessities, not within 300 feet of a bridge, tunnel, building, place where people gather, or an open fire.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: What is a safe haven, as described in the hazardous materials driving and parking rules?
choice_a: Any interstate highway rest stop
choice_b: An approved place, usually designated by local authorities, for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives
choice_c: A fenced area located only at the shipper's dock
choice_d: Any location more than 300 feet from a building
explanation: A safe haven is an approved place for parking unattended vehicles loaded with explosives, and designation of authorized safe havens is usually made by local authorities.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: If not physically inside a parked placarded vehicle, how close must the person attending it remain, keeping the vehicle in clear view?
choice_a: Within 25 feet
choice_b: Within 50 feet
choice_c: Within 100 feet
choice_d: Within 300 feet
explanation: The person attending a placarded vehicle must be in the vehicle, awake, and not in the sleeper berth, or within 100 feet of the vehicle with it in clear view.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: What should a driver use for stopped-vehicle warning signals around a tank of Class 3 (Flammable Liquids), instead of flares or fuses?
choice_a: Burning road flares only
choice_b: Reflective triangles or red electric lights
choice_c: A handheld flashlight waved by the driver
choice_d: No warning device is required for hazmat loads
explanation: Drivers must use reflective triangles or red electric lights and must never use burning signals such as flares or fuses around a tank used for Class 3 (Flammable Liquids) or Division 2.1 (Flammable Gas), or a vehicle loaded with Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: If transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, what must the driver have and follow?
choice_a: A verbal agreement with the shipper only
choice_b: A written route plan
choice_c: A GPS tracking device provided by the state
choice_d: Nothing extra beyond the standard shipping papers
explanation: Drivers transporting Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives must have a written route plan and follow it; carriers prepare the plan in advance, though the driver may plan the route if picking up explosives away from the employer's terminal, and must keep a copy while transporting the explosives.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: Within how many feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases) is smoking prohibited?
choice_a: 10 feet
choice_b: 25 feet
choice_c: 50 feet
choice_d: 100 feet
explanation: The manual prohibits smoking within 25 feet of a placarded cargo tank used for Class 3 (flammable liquids) or Division 2.1 (gases), and also prohibits smoking or carrying a lighted cigarette, cigar, or pipe within 25 feet of a vehicle containing Class 1, Class 3, Class 4.1, Class 4.2, or Class 5 materials.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: What must a driver do before fueling a motor vehicle that contains hazardous materials?
choice_a: Turn off the engine, and someone must always be at the nozzle controlling fuel flow
choice_b: Remove all placards before refueling
choice_c: Leave the engine running to keep the fuel pump powered
choice_d: Notify the National Response Center before every fueling stop
explanation: The manual requires turning off the engine before fueling a motor vehicle containing hazardous materials, and someone must always be at the nozzle, controlling fuel flow.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: What fire extinguisher rating must the power unit of a placarded vehicle carry?
choice_a: 5 B:C or more
choice_b: 10 B:C or more
choice_c: 20 A:B:C or more
choice_d: No specific rating is required, only a working extinguisher
explanation: The power unit of placarded vehicles must have a fire extinguisher with a UL rating of 10 B:C or more.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-14

question: What is the only acceptable way to check tire pressure on a placarded vehicle?
choice_a: Kicking or thumping the tire
choice_b: Visually inspecting the tire's shape
choice_c: Using a tire pressure gauge
choice_d: Checking the tire manufacturer's sticker only
explanation: The manual states the only acceptable way to check tire pressure is to use a tire pressure gauge, and drivers must examine each tire at the beginning of each trip and each time the vehicle is parked.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-15

question: Where must a driver keep hazardous materials shipping papers while behind the wheel?
choice_a: In the glove compartment, out of sight
choice_b: Within reach (with seat belt on), or in a pouch on the driver's door
choice_c: In the sleeper berth
choice_d: With the dispatcher, communicated by radio only
explanation: When behind the wheel, shipping papers must be kept within the driver's reach with the seat belt on, or in a pouch on the driver's door, so they can be easily seen by someone entering the cab.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-15

question: What special equipment must a driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks have in the vehicle?
choice_a: A spare cargo tank valve and a welding kit
choice_b: An approved gas mask and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings
choice_c: A hazmat suit rated for radioactive materials
choice_d: A secondary containment trailer
explanation: A driver transporting chlorine in cargo tanks must have an approved gas mask in the vehicle and an emergency kit for controlling leaks in dome cover plate fittings on the cargo tank.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-15

question: How far before the nearest rail must a placarded vehicle stop at a railroad crossing?
choice_a: 5 to 10 feet
choice_b: 15 to 50 feet
choice_c: 50 to 100 feet
choice_d: 100 to 200 feet
explanation: The manual requires stopping 15 to 50 feet before the nearest rail, proceeding only when sure no train is coming and the tracks can be cleared without stopping, and never shifting gears while crossing the tracks.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-15

question: Before opening the doors of a trailer that may be carrying a hazmat cargo fire, what should the driver do?
choice_a: Open the doors immediately to let smoke escape
choice_b: Feel the trailer doors to see if they are hot; if hot, do not open them
choice_c: Spray water directly on the doors regardless of temperature
choice_d: Wait exactly ten minutes before checking
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to feel trailer doors to see if they are hot before opening them; if hot, there may be a cargo fire and the doors should not be opened, since opening them lets air in and may make the fire flare up.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-16

question: In a breakdown or accident involving Division 1.1, 1.2, or 1.3 explosives, how far from the vehicles and occupied buildings should the explosives be placed before separating vehicles involved in a collision?
choice_a: At least 50 feet
choice_b: At least 100 feet
choice_c: At least 200 feet
choice_d: At least 500 feet
explanation: The manual instructs drivers to remove all explosives before separating vehicles involved in a collision and place the explosives at least 200 feet from the vehicles and occupied buildings, staying a safe distance away.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-16

question: How should a driver try to identify a leaking hazardous material if the source is not obvious?
choice_a: By carefully smelling the leaking substance
choice_b: By touching a small amount to check its texture
choice_c: Never by touching or smelling it; use shipping papers, labels, or package location instead
choice_d: By tasting a diluted sample
explanation: The manual warns never to try to identify a leaking material or find the source of a leak by smell, since toxic gases can destroy the sense of smell and can injure or kill even if they don't smell; the driver should identify the material using shipping papers, labels, or package location and never touch leaking material.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-16

question: If hazardous materials are spilling from a driver's vehicle, what is the correct sequence of actions listed in the manual?
choice_a: Keep driving to the nearest phone, then report the spill
choice_b: Park it, secure the area, stay there, and call for help or send someone else for help
choice_c: Transfer the remaining cargo to another vehicle immediately
choice_d: Wash the spill away with water before anyone arrives
explanation: The manual instructs that when hazardous materials are spilling from a vehicle, the driver should park it, secure the area, stay there, and call for help or send someone else for help, never continuing to drive to find a phone or similar reason.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-16

question: Which of the following requires phoning the National Response Center as a direct result of a hazardous materials incident?
choice_a: Estimated property damage exceeds $50,000
choice_b: The driver is delayed by traffic for more than 30 minutes
choice_c: The shipment is one day late for delivery
choice_d: The shipping papers contain a minor spelling error
explanation: Required notification triggers include a death, an injury requiring hospitalization, estimated property damage exceeding $50,000, a public evacuation of more than one hour, closure of a major transportation artery for an hour or more, and certain fire, spillage, or contamination events; the National Response Center's number is (800) 424-8802.
source_note: Connecticut CDL Manual (R-295 Rev. 12/2024, AAMVA 2022 Modernized CDL Testing System), Connecticut Department of Motor Vehicles, Section 9 - Hazardous Materials, p. 9-17
